rv.q: Here is a particularly frustrating example of an at least five-star performance of an at best three-star script.
The actual play can't really live up to the magnificence of the setting.
Ferguson leans into all of Tru’s Southern camp charisma without caricaturing it.
A terrific, poignant performance and a set that deserves applause of its own, but the play itself doesn’t quite fill the space.
But the narrative is aimless, descending into moony reminiscences of Tru’s childhood friendship with his aunt, the time he first got drunk at seven and was bitten by a cottonmouth snake aged eight.
But the play itself – largely an hour and a half of self-indulgent ramblings – lacks purpose, shape and dynamic.
Jesse Tyler Ferguson captures the In Cold Blood author’s self-loathing and hubris, but even he can’t save this shapeless monologue.
Ferguson is captivating in the role: camp, catty, and totally unapologetic.
Tru delivers a beautifully realised evening in the company of one of the great wits of the last century, led by an understatedly magnetic Ferguson.
Ashford has chosen to make this element of the script explicit, to great effect.
Jesse Tyler Ferguson, best known for his role in Modern Family, seems born to play the role.
This play may not offer anything new, but it is a star vehicle, and Ferguson does not disappoint.
So while Ferguson may be an immaculate Capote, the vehicle he is in relies a lot on the audience being devotees who can fill in its blanks for themselves.
Tru is a magnificent production, guided by Rob Ashford’s direction and anchored by Tyler Ferguson’s faultless performance.
Tru is a chance to see a performer at the top of their game and to be blown away by their sheer magnificence.
The set, the actor’s spontaneity, and his rapport with the audience when he engaged meant that I was mesmerized.
Ultimately, Truman Capote is a alcoholic, name-dropping narcissist, and Jesse Tyler Ferguson’s portrayal of him is brilliant.
That said, Ferguson’s rich and dynamic individual performance soars in an engrossing delivery that never falters.
Staging TRU in such intimate fashion gives the audience a front-row seat into a world of royal scandal and power couple infidelities that plays on much that still feels relevant to today's world.
An extraordinary transformation and a convincing Capote can’t quite overcome a play in which too little happens.

cn.t: Ferguson captivates in a stunning immersive production, but critics find the 1989 monologue itself thin and shapeless. Farnsworth's spectacular apartment set earns universal praise, while the play struggles to match the five-star performance.
